entities.name: Puxian Wannu
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Púxiān Wànnú was a Jurchen warlord who established the short-lived Eastern Xia dynasty in 13th-century China.

As the grandson of the founder of the Jin dynasty, Puxian Wannu's rise to power was shaped by the tumultuous politics of the region, particularly the struggles between the Mongols and the Southern Song.

His reign was marked by a series of military campaigns against the Mongols, as well as efforts to consolidate power and establish a stable administrative system.

Despite his efforts, the Eastern Xia dynasty ultimately collapsed in 1233, succumbing to the Mongol conquests that would soon engulf the region.

In the centuries that followed, Puxian Wannu's legacy was all but forgotten, until recent scholarship shed new light on the life and reign of this enigmatic figure.

As a testament to his enduring influence, the city of Puxian Wannu, in modern-day Shanxi province, remains a reminder of the complex web of alliances and rivalries that shaped the medieval world.

The inscriptions on the Puxian Wannu stele, discovered in 1932, provide a poignant glimpse into the life and times of this forgotten warlord, offering a unique window into the cultural and historical context of late imperial China.
